Yeah, I mean, you hit the nail on the head there. It's definitely bleeding into both sides of my life, which is why I'm sitting here talking to you.

I can tell she doesn't trust that I'm actually absorbing a single word she's saying. And when those family plans don't go the way they should because I missed a detail I talked over, or because I blurted out something that derailed the whole conversation... man, she gets so upset. 

So yeah, I'm managing, the ship is sailing, but I'm definitely burning goodwill on both ends. It just feels like I have to do damage control every single week, whether it's buying lunch for the office to smooth over a rough meeting where I was too antsy, or apologizing to my wife because I steamrolled our evening. It's exhausting having to constantly apologize for how I operate.

Just going a mile a minute under the table. Or I'll grab a pen—I always have these nice metal pens we got made with the company logo—and I'll just be clicking it. Click, click, click. I don't even hear it half the time, but apparently, it's loud enough because people have started giving me these... these looks, you know? Like they think I'm impatient or trying to rush them through their presentations. And the thing is, I'm not! I'm actually trying really hard to pay attention to what they're saying about the quarterly projections or whatever, but I'm just constantly shifting around in my chair, trying to get comfortable, crossing my legs, uncrossing them, leaning forward, leaning back. \n\nIt's like I have this built-up energy that just has to go somewhere, and if I'm stuck in a chair, it comes out in my hands or my feet. Yes, I do. I'm actually trying really hard to pay attention to what they're saying about the quarterly projections or whatever, but I'm just constantly shifting around in my chair, trying to get comfortable, crossing my legs, uncrossing them, leaning forward, leaning back. \n\nIt's like I have this built-up energy that just has to go somewhere, and if I'm stuck in a chair, it comes out in my hands or my feet. And it's embarrassing, honestly, because I'm supposed to be setting the tone for the room, right? I'm the CEO. But instead, I'm over there squirming like a kid who needs to use the restroom, and my VP of Sales is giving me the side-eye because he thinks I'm blowing off his numbers.\n\nDoctor: Do you often act impulsively, like interrupting people or blurt out answers before they finish?\n\nPatient: Oh, man... yeah. Yes, I do. And it's honestly becoming a real problem because I can tell it really rubs people the wrong way. \n\nLike at work, I’ll be in one of those meetings I was just talking about, and someone—let's say my operations manager, Dave. So he'll be halfway through a sentence about, I don't know, supply chain logistics or vendor delays, and I just... I can't wait for him to get to the end of it. I just blurt out the end of his thought. I literally just finish his sentence for him so we can keep things moving. And I see his face drop, and I know it rubs him the wrong way. It rubs a lot of my employees the wrong way because they probably think I'm this arrogant boss who doesn't value their input, but it's really just that my brain is already three steps ahead and the words just fall out of my mouth.\n\nAnd it's not even just at the office, which is the worst part. It’s happening at home, too. Like I mentioned my in-laws earlier? My wife will be on the phone with her parents—or worse, we'll be on a FaceTime call with them, which we do every Sunday evening because her mom insists on seeing the house and what we're doing with it—and my wife will be right in the middle of telling them a story about her week, or explaining our plans for their visit, and I just jump right in. I'll just completely cut her off and take over the conversation, or I'll jump in to correct some minor, totally unimportant detail she got wrong about the timeline. \n\nI don't even mean to be rude! Yeah, exactly. Looking back, this was exactly how it was when I was a kid, too. It was never about me staring off into space or daydreaming or losing focus. I knew exactly what was going on in class. So yeah, it was always the overly active, impulsive stuff. Never the attention. It's like I've been running on this exact same motor since I was a little kid, just... now I'm doing it in executive meetings instead of a classroom.

I just blurted things out because the answer was already in my head and I couldn't hold it in for the extra five seconds it would take for her to finish her sentence. I can tell she doesn't trust that I'm actually absorbing a single word she's saying. Wait, I feel like I'm repeating myself a bit here, or maybe I misunderstood you, but no. No, definitely not inattention. Like I was just saying, it’s the complete opposite. The inattention is literally a non-issue for me. Zero.

I would just get up without asking, just stand up and wander around the room to see what someone else was doing or go look at the pencil sharpener, completely oblivious to the fact that you're supposed to sit still during a lesson. \n\nAnd the blurting things out—man, that was a huge issue for me back then. A teacher would be standing up there at the chalkboard, halfway through asking the class a question, and I would just shout the answer out before they even finished the sentence. I couldn't even wait for them to finish talking, let alone raise my hand and sit there quietly waiting to be called on. The thought would just fire off in my brain and shoot right out of my mouth before I could even think about stopping it. \n\nSo yeah, to be completely clear, I wasn't daydreaming or spacing out at all back then. I wasn't inattentive. I was just a human pinball bouncing off the walls. It was always the physical energy and just doing things before I thought about them.\n\nDoctor: Before age 12, did you also have trouble staying focused on schoolwork or listening to the teacher, or was it mainly the hyperactive and impulsive behavior?\n\nPatient: Yeah, so, like I was just saying a second ago, it really was strictly the hyperactive and impulsive stuff. I had absolutely zero trouble listening to the teachers or focusing on the actual schoolwork. In fact, it was almost the exact opposite. I listened so well and picked things up so fast that I'd finish whatever worksheet or assignment they handed out in two minutes flat, and then I'd just be sitting there with absolutely nothing to do. And of course, that's when the trouble would start, because I couldn't just sit there quietly. \n\nI remember specifically in fourth grade, I had this teacher, Mrs. Gable. Strict older woman, always wore this incredibly strong floral perfume you could smell from down the hall. She was absolutely convinced I never listened to a word she said because I was never looking at her. One time, she was doing this whole long lesson on fractions on the overhead projector, and I was literally under my desk. I had found a loose screw on the metal leg of the chair and I was trying to tighten it with a paperclip. She stopped the whole class, completely silent, and called my name, obviously trying to catch me not paying attention to make an example out of me. She asked me what the common denominator was for whatever she had just put on the board. And without even pulling my head out from under the desk, I just rattled off the exact right answer. \n\nI didn't have trouble focusing on the work. Honestly, the work was usually just way too slow. I didn't need them to repeat things three times for me to get it. So while they were droning on for the rest of the class, my brain was already ten steps ahead. I think my body was just doing its own thing—tapping, moving, talking, taking apart my pens—because I was under-stimulated by the pace, not because I couldn't focus. I absorbed everything. My brain just didn't require me to be glued to a chair, facing forward with my hands folded, to process the information, you know? So no, staying focused on the lessons was never the problem back then. It was one hundred percent just the fact that I couldn't contain my physical energy while they were teaching.\n\nDoctor: Before age 12, did you also have trouble paying attention or were you mainly just hyperactive and impulsive?\n\nPatient: I feel like we might be going in circles here a bit, Doc, because it really is exactly what I was just telling you about! I would get up without asking, just wander over to the bookshelf or go look out the window or inspect the pencil sharpener while they were right in the middle of a lesson. It just didn't even register in my brain that I was supposed to ask permission to use my own legs, you know? I'd just do it. \n\nAnd the blurting things out... man, that was my signature move. A teacher would be halfway through a question, and I’d just shout the answer out before they even finished the sentence. I just couldn't hold it in. The thought would hit my brain and bypass any sort of filter or waiting period. So, yeah, like I said, it was definitely just the physical energy and the impulsivity, never an issue with actually paying attention to what was going on. I was paying attention to everything, I just couldn't sit still or keep my mouth shut while I was doing it.\n\nDoctor: Aside from the recent distractibility you described, do you still have ongoing problems with paying attention in everyday life?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I do. It’s actually incredibly frustrating, especially given my role. You know, when you’re running the company, people expect you to be the guy with all the answers, the guy who catches every single little detail. And I try, I really do.
